Onychomycosis

Two sham-controlled trials found no improvement in onychomycosis cure with the tested 1064-nm Nd:YAG protocols. Small uncontrolled laser studies sometimes report visible improvement, but fungal testing and co-treatments limit interpretation, and clinical efficacy of low-dose PBM remains unestablished.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two sham-controlled trials found no improvement in onychomycosis cure with the tested 1064-nm Nd:YAG protocols. Small uncontrolled laser studies sometimes report visible improvement, but fungal testing and co-treatments limit interpretation, and clinical efficacy of low-dose PBM remains unestablished.

Summary of the Evidence

Seven publications address onychomycosis: six human clinical reports and one in-vitro study. The human evidence includes two randomized sham-controlled trials and four non-randomized reports. Most clinical procedures used 1064-nm Nd:YAG, class-IV, or CO₂ lasers, whose thermal or ablative effects differ from low-dose PBM. One uncontrolled study combined a multiwavelength class-IV laser with mechanical abrasion, so improvement cannot be attributed to light alone.

Human and clinical evidence

Two sham-controlled trials tested short-pulse 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser. In a 51-person trial, the laser group did not have a better cure result than placebo (Sabbah et al. 2019). In the quadruple-blind LASER-1 trial, 64 people with diabetes were randomized and 63 analyzed; after four sessions and one year of follow-up, clinical and microbiological cure did not differ from sham. One subungual hematoma was reported (Nijenhuis-Rosien et al. 2019). These results do not show benefit for the tested 1064-nm protocols, while the safety observation applies to the trial’s specific regimen.

Other clinical reports are less conclusive. A small prospective study combined 650-, 810-, and 915-nm class-IV laser exposure with mechanical abrasion and reported some clinical improvement, but fungal tests remained positive in many nails. Retrospective and uncontrolled Nd:YAG reports also describe changes in nail appearance, which are not equivalent to confirmed fungal eradication. The study designs and outcomes vary, and they do not supply a reliable estimate of PBM-specific cure.

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified in this category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One in-vitro study exposed Trichophyton rubrum to 405-nm blue visible light and reported reactive-oxygen-related fungal membrane damage (Li et al. 2025). This high-fluence antifungal experiment is a laboratory result; it does not show that light can reach or eradicate fungus under a human nail using a clinical PBM protocol.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The controlled clinical trials used short-pulse 1064-nm near-infrared Nd:YAG laser. The multiwavelength pilot used 650-nm red visible, 810-nm near-infrared, and 915-nm near-infrared light alongside nail abrasion. The laboratory study used 405-nm blue light at a high fluence. These are different light ranges, devices, and mechanisms. No clinical dose-finding study establishes an effective low-dose PBM wavelength or dose for fungal cure.

Interpretation

The strongest direct clinical evidence is negative for the tested 1064-nm Nd:YAG regimens: neither sham-controlled trial showed improved cure. Uncontrolled studies report some visible nail changes, but those results do not outweigh the controlled fungal and clinical outcomes, especially when another procedure was used at the same time. Laboratory blue-light activity is not yet evidence of a clinical PBM treatment.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate evidence that tested 1064-nm Nd:YAG protocols did not improve cure versus sham Very low for clinical benefit from low-dose PBM specifically
Publications and records7 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two blinded sham-controlled trials found no better clinical or fungal cure with the tested 1064-nm Nd:YAG protocols, which supports a conclusion about those specific regimens. Most other clinical reports used thermal or ablative lasers, often with abrasion, so they do not directly test low-dose PBM. A well-powered trial of clearly dosed PBM with both clinical and fungal outcomes would address that gap.
